[PAPER_0050, relevance_score=0.355] Specifically, our first preregistered hypothesis (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/HMNA5) stated that the regulator's empathic accuracy would predict the effectiveness of interpersonal emotion regulation provided by them. Accuracy was operationalized as the difference (reversed-scored) between regulators' perceptions of their partners' emotions from the ground truth-the actual emotional ratings given by the targets. Effectiveness was operationalized as the match between what a target thought would be effective and what a regulator said they would do to be effective.

[PAPER_0051, relevance_score=0.405] Our second preregistered hypothesis was that individual differences in regulators' emotional clarity would positively predict their empathic accuracy, which would, in turn, predict the effectiveness of their interpersonal emotion regulation. In addition to our main preregistered hypotheses, we also explored the associations between regulators' emotional intimacy, attachment orientations, empathic accuracy, and effectiveness of interpersonal emotion regulation.

[PAPER_0094, relevance_score=0.331] Hypothesis 2: Does Regulators' Clarity Predict Empathic Accuracy?

We preregistered and conducted a simple linear regression analysis to examine whether the empathic accuracy of regulators would be predicted by their clarity of emotional experience scores. We found a significant association between emotional clarity and empathic accuracy, t(91) = 2.06, p < .05. As predicted, participants with higher emotional clarity scores tend to have a higher empathic accuracy (b = 0.09, β = .21), 95% CI for b [.003, .180].

[PAPER_0095, relevance_score=0.223] Here, emotional clarity explained approximately 5% of the variance in empathic accuracy (R2 = .045). This association remained significant when we controlled for relationship duration, age, gender, and racial background of the regulator, p < .05.

The Indirect Effect of Clarity on the Effectiveness of Interpersonal Emotion Regulation

We also preregistered the hypothesis that the regulator's emotional clarity would predict the effectiveness of their emotion regulation attempts through their empathic accuracy.

[PREREG_0001, relevance_score=0.253] Title: Emotion Perception and Extrinsic Regulation in Couples

Description: Romantic partners influence one another's emotional experiences. When one partner attempts to modify the emotions of the other, extrinsic emotion regulation takes place. Extrinsic regulation aims to reduce negative emotions and increase the positive emotions of a target. Factors that contribute to the effectiveness of extrinsic regulation remain unexplored. The proposed study will investigate whether accuracy in the perception of a partner's emotions predicts successful extrinsic regulation.

[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.446] Method

Participants

We collected dyadic data from both partners in a romantic relationship in an online survey study conducted through Prolific. Our preregistered sample size of 100 dyads was based on prior work's sample size (Gregory et al., 2020), observed effects, and our resources. However, considering attrition rates inherent in dyadic studies, we recruited 109 individuals on Prolific who also had romantic partners with Prolific accounts who also indicated an initial interest in participating.

[PAPER_0056, relevance_score=0.303] Only three couples had been together for less than 1 year. Among 92 couples, 78 were in opposite-sex relationships and nine couples were in same-sex relationships. Participants were compensated with $3.50 for their completion of the study.

We randomly assigned one member of each couple to act as a regulator (Nmales = 41, Nfemales = 49, Nnonbinary = 1) and the other to act as the target (Nmales = 44, Nfemales = 44, Nnonbinary = 3) in the emotion regulation procedure.

[PAPER_0087, relevance_score=0.399] Procedure

We created two separate online surveys for targets and regulators on Qualtrics. After each partner was assigned to the role of a target or regulator, we shared the link for the regulator survey with regulator partners and the target survey with target partners on Prolific. All partners were first presented with a consent form. We asked partners to refrain from discussing their answers with each other until after they both completed the surveys. Each partner read a vignette, rated the eight emotions in line with the instruction they were provided, and answered one open-ended question about the strategy they would expect/provide.

Extrinsic regulation aims to reduce negative emotions and increase the positive emotions of a target. Factors that contribute to the effectiveness of extrinsic regulation remain unexplored. The proposed study will investigate whether accuracy in the perception of a partner's emotions predicts successful extrinsic regulation.

[PAPER_0015, relevance_score=0.221] Targets were then asked to describe what their partner could say to help them feel good or better in each situation, using an open-ended response format. The regulators were asked to describe what they would say to their partners to help them feel good or better in each situation. Accuracy was defined as the mean difference in ratings between the regulator's estimates of their partner's emotions and their actual emotion ratings across the scenarios. Effectiveness of regulation was defined as the mean score of similarity between regulator's open-ended responses and target's open-ended responses as rated by independent coders.

[PAPER_0069, relevance_score=0.258] Supplemental Materials , we provide additional details on empathic accuracy subscores calculated on individual emotions. For ease of interpretation, we converted this difference score to an accuracy score by subtracting the difference score from five as the last step so that higher scores would indicate higher accuracy and lower scores would indicate lower accuracy.

The absolute difference score as an operationalization of empathic accuracy was preregistered for the present study.

[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.306] Method

Participants

We collected dyadic data from both partners in a romantic relationship in an online survey study conducted through Prolific. Our preregistered sample size of 100 dyads was based on prior work's sample size (Gregory et al., 2020), observed effects, and our resources. However, considering attrition rates inherent in dyadic studies, we recruited 109 individuals on Prolific who also had romantic partners with Prolific accounts who also indicated an initial interest in participating.

[PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.270] Of these 109 potential couples, there were 92 couples (N = 184) in which both members of the couples completed the study. We then did a power analysis using G*power (Faul et al., 2009), which indicated that 92 participants could reliably detect a .28 effect size at a .80 power level with linear regression, an effect size smaller than that found in prior work on which we based our planned sample size (Gregory et al., 2020).
